sites.name: Leicester
sites.text: One of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw, and the start of the Soar variant. Æthelflæd of Mercia took it back from the Danes in 918.

sites.name: Heath Wood, Ingleby
sites.text: The only known Viking cremation cemetery in Britain: around 60 barrows in the wood above the Trent, on the first stage of the Way.

sites.name: Repton
sites.text: Where the Way begins, up the Trent from Derby. The Great Heathen Army wintered here in 873–874 and drove out the Mercian king; a Viking camp and burials have been excavated by the church.

sites.name: Derby
sites.text: One of the Five Boroughs. Its name is Old Norse, Djúrabý, "deer farm". Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, took it back from the Danes in 917.

sites.name: Nottingham
sites.text: Another of the Five Boroughs. The Great Heathen Army wintered here in 867–868.

sites.name: Stow Minster
sites.text: Off the route, 5 km from Torksey. A great Anglo-Saxon minster with the earliest known carving of a Viking ship in England scratched into a pillar.

sites.name: Torksey
sites.text: The Great Army's winter camp of 872–873, where the Fossdyke meets the Trent. Excavation and metal-detecting have found thousands of finds: hack silver, weights and lead gaming pieces.

sites.name: Fossdyke
sites.text: A canal joining the Trent at Torksey to the Witham at Lincoln, probably Roman and still navigable.

sites.name: Gainsborough
sites.text: On the Trent north of Torksey. Sweyn Forkbeard, king of Denmark, made it his base when he conquered England in 1013 and died there in 1014.

sites.name: Lincoln
sites.text: One of the Five Boroughs, with a busy Viking-age mint. Lincoln was the chief town of Lindsey, the old kingdom that the Danes divided into three ridings, from the Old Norse þriðjungr, a third: the Lindsey Ridings take their name from them. The Lindsey Ridings leaves north-east for Grimsby and the Humber coast.

sites.name: Stamford
sites.text: The fifth of the Five Boroughs, on the Welland, with a Danish fortified borough north of the river. The route turns down the Welland here into Holland.

sites.name: Crowland
sites.text: Crowland Abbey stands in the Fens by the Welland. Later medieval chronicles claimed the Danes burned it in 870, though that account is now thought unreliable.

sites.name: Bardney Abbey
sites.text: A royal monastery of Lindsey and Mercia, the shrine of St Oswald. It was destroyed by the Danes around 870 and not refounded until after the Norman Conquest.

sites.name: Skegness
sites.text: Where the Lindsey coastal route and the Skegness route meet the sea. Its name is Old Norse: Skeggi's ness, the headland of a man called Skeggi.

sites.name: Lincolnshire Wolds
sites.text: Tealby, Normanby, Grimsby and dozens more: Lincolnshire has more Old Norse -by place names than any other English county, many of them strung along these chalk hills. The Lindsey Ridings cross their western edge at Caistor, close to the Viking Way footpath.

sites.name: Barton-upon-Humber
sites.text: The old ferry town on the south bank of the Humber. St Peter's Church has an Anglo-Saxon tower from around the end of the 10th century.

sites.name: Grimsby
sites.text: On the Humber coast: by tradition named after Grim, a Danish fisherman, with the Old Norse -by for farm or village. The Lindsey Ridings reaches the sea here.

sites.name: Humber
sites.text: The estuary the Great Army crossed on its way to York in 866. The Lindsey Ridings looks over Trent Falls at Alkborough, where the Trent and the Ouse meet to form the Humber.

sites.name: Leeds
sites.text: Leeds Minster keeps a 10th-century Anglo-Scandinavian stone cross carved with Weland the Smith, a hero of Norse legend. Start of the Aire variant.

sites.name: Castleford
sites.text: In 948 the army of Viking York under Eric Bloodaxe caught King Eadred's rearguard here and slaughtered it, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records.

sites.name: Selby
sites.text: A name of Old Norse origin, probably "willow farm", like many -by places along the Way.

sites.name: Riccall
sites.text: Harald Hardrada's fleet came up the Ouse and landed here in September 1066, the last great Viking invasion of England.

sites.name: Fulford
sites.text: Harald Hardrada beat the northern earls here on 20 September 1066, five days before his defeat at Stamford Bridge.

sites.name: Stamford Bridge
sites.text: Where the Way ends, east of York. Harold Godwinson defeated and killed Harald Hardrada here on 25 September 1066, the end of the Viking Age in England.

sites.name: Barnby Dun
sites.text: Old Norse names line the Don below Doncaster: Barnby is Bjarni's farm, with the Norse -by, and Kirk Sandall takes the Norse kirkja, church.

sites.name: Beverley
sites.text: The Minster stands on the monastery of St John of Beverley, which by tradition the Danes destroyed around 866. Later kings of England, Athelstan first, honoured his shrine as they fought to win back the North.

sites.name: Danes' Dyke
sites.text: The great earthwork across Flamborough Head, east of Bridlington. Despite the name it is much older than the Vikings: it was dug in prehistory, and the Danes were credited with it later.

sites.name: Tadcaster
sites.text: Harold Godwinson gathered his army here on 24 September 1066 after marching north from London, then went through York to beat Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge the next day.

sites.name: York
sites.text: Jorvik. The Great Heathen Army took it on 1 November 866, and it was the capital of a Viking kingdom until Eric Bloodaxe was driven out in 954.

sites.name: Brompton
sites.text: St Thomas's Church keeps a famous group of hogback stones: Anglo-Scandinavian grave markers of the 10th century, carved as houses with bears at each end.

sites.name: Teesside
sites.text: The Tees was near the northern edge of Scandinavian settlement, and the names show it: Ormesby, Normanby, Lazenby and Maltby all end in the Old Norse -by, a farm or village.

sites.name: Ratae (Leicester)
sites.text: Ratae Corieltauvorum. The Jewry Wall, part of the town's public baths, is one of the largest pieces of Roman civic building still standing in Britain.

sites.name: Derventio (Little Chester, Derby)
sites.text: A Roman fort and small town on the Derwent, where the road from the south crossed the river north of Derby's centre.

sites.name: Margidunum
sites.text: A Roman small town on the Fosse Way above the Trent at East Bridgford, close to the Way at Gunthorpe.

sites.name: Ad Pontem
sites.text: A small Roman town on the Fosse Way by the Trent at Thorpe, near Newark.

sites.name: Great Casterton
sites.text: A small walled Roman town on Ermine Street, the Roman road from London to Lincoln and York. North of Stamford the Great North Road follows its line.

sites.name: Durobrivae (Water Newton)
sites.text: A walled Roman town on Ermine Street by the Nene, south of Stamford. The Water Newton treasure found here is the earliest Christian church silver known from the Roman Empire.

sites.name: Causennae (Ancaster)
sites.text: A small walled Roman town on Ermine Street, east of the Great North Road at Grantham.

sites.name: Lindum (Lincoln)
sites.text: A legionary fortress, then a colonia for retired soldiers. Newport Arch, its Roman north gate, still has traffic passing through it.

sites.name: Segelocum (Littleborough)
sites.text: Where the Roman road from Lincoln to Doncaster and York crossed the Trent, opposite Marton on the Way.

sites.name: Caistor
sites.text: A small Roman walled town on the edge of the Wolds; pieces of its wall survive near the church.

sites.name: Danum (Doncaster)
sites.text: A Roman fort guarding the crossing of the Don on the road north to York, under the town centre by the Minster.

sites.name: Templeborough (Rotherham)
sites.text: A Roman fort beside the Don between Sheffield and Rotherham. Its site now lies under the Magna science centre and the old steelworks.

sites.name: Lagentium (Castleford)
sites.text: A Roman fort and settlement where the road north crossed the Aire.

sites.name: Petuaria (Brough)
sites.text: A Roman town at the Humber crossing. An inscription found here records a magistrate's gift of a new stage for its theatre.

sites.name: Calcaria (Tadcaster)
sites.text: The Roman settlement where the road from York to the west crossed the Wharfe.

sites.name: Eboracum (York)
sites.text: The legionary fortress and capital of northern Britain. Constantine was proclaimed emperor here in 306.

sites.name: Isurium Brigantum (Aldborough)
sites.text: The Roman town of the Brigantes, west of the Great North Road at Boroughbridge, with mosaics still in place.
